title: The Physics of Unresolved Uncertainty: Quantum Mechanics as a Theory of Potentiality
abstract: We propose a reformulation of quantum mechanics as a theory of unresolved uncertainty. The framework is formulated in the language of complex-valued measure theory, regarded as a pre-probabilistic counterpart of ordinary probability theory. In this formulation, additivity, conditioning, independence, mixtures, transition kernels, and temporal divisibility retain natural linear forms at the potentiality level, while non-classical probability-level features such as interference arise from the nonlinear Born map. Measurement is described as Bayesian-type conditioning of potentialities on actualized information, and non-selective measurement as the replacement of coherent potentiality by statistical mixtures of conditional branches. Mixed states, decoherence, composite systems, entanglement, and Bell-type correlations are also given a unified potentiality-level interpretation. The resulting formulation is empirically equivalent to standard quantum mechanics, but it makes explicit a pre-probabilistic description of physical reality that is usually implicit in the Hilbert-space formalism.
summary: The paper proposes reformulating quantum mechanics as a 'Theory of Potentiality' using complex-valued measure theory. It distinguishes between the linear mathematics governing unactualized potentialities and the nonlinear Born map that yields observable probabilities. This framework aims to provide a deeper, pre-probabilistic understanding of QM while remaining mathematically equivalent to standard formalism.
main_problem: To reformulate quantum mechanics (QM) as a fundamental theory of 'unresolved uncertainty' rather than solely focusing on probabilities derived from actualized outcomes.
main_result: The proposed potentiality framework is empirically equivalent to standard QM but makes explicit the pre-probabilistic structure underlying quantum phenomena like interference and entanglement.
method: It utilizes complex-valued measure theory, treating potentialities as primary objects that retain linear additivity, contrasting this with the nonlinear Born map required for observable probabilities.
model_or_system: The model describes general quantum systems using potentiality distributions ($\psi$), which are complex-valued measures over an underlying context space $\Omega$. It systematically maps standard QM concepts (e.g., partial trace, Lüders update) to analogous structures in this new formalism.
key_observables: Observable probabilities ($p_X(x)$), coherent potentiality aggregates ($P(A)$), and the structure of joint potentialities ($\psi(x, y)$).
important_parameters: The distinction between linear (potentiality) and quadratic (probability/Born map) structures is key; no specific physical parameters are emphasized over the mathematical formalism.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that QM can be fundamentally understood as a theory of pre-probabilistic potentialities, which requires redefining primitive notions away from standard probability axioms.
figures_summary: A detailed comparison table maps standard quantum mechanical concepts (e.g., density matrix, Lüders update) to their corresponding structures within the Theory of Potentiality.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops a 'potentiality language,' contrasting it with standard QM by defining analogues for core probabilistic operations (conditioning, independence) at the complex measure level before applying the Born map.
why_interesting: This work offers a deep conceptual re-foundation of quantum mechanics that addresses the measurement problem by positing an underlying mathematical structure of unresolved potentiality, which is highly relevant to foundational questions in open quantum systems theory.
